# How to use this guide

Social and Preventive Pharmacy is a theory subject with no numericals. Marks come from **well-organised descriptive answers**: definitions, classifications, tables and the "objectives → functioning → outcome → pharmacist's role" frame for national programmes. Study one unit a day: read the notes, make your own one-page chart of each programme or disease, then answer the question bank aloud or in writing.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus for BP802T. No unit was split or joined. Unit 2 (diseases) and Units 3–4 (national programmes) carry the most marks.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The question bank has long (10-mark), short (5-mark) and a few very short (2-mark) questions for each unit, and at least 10 MCQs per unit.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare a full, structured answer.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Health and disease | WHO definition and dimensions of health, levels of prevention, balanced diet, vitamin deficiencies, malnutrition (PEM), urbanisation and poverty, personal hygiene |
| 2 Preventive medicine | Malaria, dengue, cholera, filariasis, hypertension, diabetes, cancer, drug addiction; any one disease as "prevention and control" |
| 3 Programmes I | NACP, NTEP, UIP, Pulse Polio, NLEP, NMHP, IDSP, NPCB&VI, NPPCD |
| 4 Programmes II | RMNCH+A schemes, family welfare and contraceptive methods, NTCP and COTPA, malaria programme history and elimination framework, NPHCE, role of WHO |
| 5 Community services | Functions of PHC, primary health care principles and elements, rural sanitation, NUHM, school health services, health education methods |

**A note on dates and targets**

Programme names, launch years and targets change. The years in these notes were checked on official sources (mohfw.gov.in, nhm.gov.in, programme sites and government press releases). Before the exam, check whether any programme has been renamed or given a new target on mohfw.gov.in or nhm.gov.in. If you are not sure of a year in the exam hall, write the objective in words — a wrong date costs more than a missing one.

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Programme answers:** use headings — Introduction (year, nodal agency) → Objectives → Components/strategies (as a numbered list or table) → Outcome → Role of pharmacist. Even if you forget a detail, the structure earns marks.
2. **Disease answers:** agent → spread → features → diagnosis → prevention and control (source, route, host) → pharmacist's role. Add a small vector or chain-of-infection diagram.
3. **Draw simple diagrams:** epidemiological triad, natural history of disease, levels of prevention, chain of infection, rural health set-up, continuum of care, poverty–disease cycle.
4. **Tables score well:** vitamin deficiencies, marasmus vs kwashiorkor, levels of prevention, COTPA sections, contraceptive methods, IDSP S/P/L forms, population norms of SC/PHC/CHC.
5. **Always end with the pharmacist's role** — this is a pharmacy paper, and examiners look for it.
6. **Learn a few key numbers exactly:** SC 5,000/3,000, PHC 30,000/20,000, CHC 1,20,000/80,000; SAM criteria; child fast-breathing cut-offs 60/50/40; hypertension 140/90; diabetes FPG 126 mg/dl; quit line 1800-11-2356; Tele-MANAS 14416.
7. **No drug doses are needed.** Name the type of treatment used in national guidelines (ORS, ACT, MDT, ART) and focus on prevention.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, prepare these five answers in full: **levels of prevention with examples**, **prevention and control of malaria (or dengue)**, **NTEP or NACP (objectives, components, pharmacist's role)**, **RMNCH+A / family welfare**, and **functions of the PHC with primary health care principles**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Unit 1 — health, nutrition, society**

| Topic | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| WHO definition (1948) | Complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease |
| Triad | Agent – host – environment; NCDs are multifactorial |
| Levels of prevention | Primordial (stop risk factors) → primary (vaccines, safe water) → secondary (screening) → tertiary (rehabilitation) |
| Leavell and Clark | Health promotion, specific protection, early diagnosis and treatment, disability limitation, rehabilitation |
| Eradication | Worldwide end (smallpox); elimination = regional or below a set level |
| Vitamin A | Night blindness, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia |
| Niacin | Pellagra: dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia |
| Folate | Megaloblastic anaemia, neural tube defects |
| Kwashiorkor vs marasmus | Oedema present vs absent |
| SAM (6–59 months) | WHZ < −3 SD, or MUAC < 115 mm, or bilateral pitting oedema |
| Poverty | Vicious cycle: poverty → disease → loss of income → poverty |

**Unit 2 — diseases**

| Disease | Agent / vector | Prevention in one line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cholera | *V. cholerae* O1, O139; faecal–oral | ORS, safe water, sanitation, hand washing, oral vaccine in high-risk areas |
| SARS | SARS-CoV; droplets | Isolation, quarantine, PPE, hand hygiene |
| Ebola | Filovirus; body fluids | Isolation, PPE, safe burial, 21-day contact follow-up, vaccine for contacts |
| Influenza | Orthomyxovirus; droplets | Yearly vaccine (drift), cough etiquette, antivirals for high-risk |
| Child pneumonia | *S. pneumoniae*, Hib, RSV | Vaccines, breastfeeding, clean fuel; fast breathing 60/50/40 |
| Malaria | *Plasmodium*; *Anopheles* (night) | Test and treat, IRS, LLIN, fish, source reduction |
| Dengue | 4 serotypes; *Aedes* (day, clean water) | Weekly emptying of containers; paracetamol, no NSAIDs |
| Chikungunya | Alphavirus; *Aedes* | As dengue; severe joint pain |
| Filariasis | *W. bancrofti*; *Culex* | Annual MDA + morbidity management |
| Hypertension | ≥ 140/90 | Salt < 5 g/day, weight, exercise, screening, adherence |
| Diabetes | FPG ≥ 126; HbA1c ≥ 6.5% | Diet, activity, screening, foot and eye care |
| Cancer | Tobacco, HPV, alcohol | Tobacco control, HPV vaccine, screen oral/breast/cervix |
| Substance abuse | Dependence, tolerance, withdrawal | NDPS Act 1985; supply, demand, harm reduction |

**Units 3 and 4 — programmes (years checked on official sources)**

| Programme | Year(s) | Key words |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NACP / NACO | NACO 1992; phase V 2021–26 | ICTC, PPTCT, ART, targeted interventions, 95-95-95, HIV/AIDS Act 2017 |
| NTEP | RNTCP 1997 → NTEP January 2020 | Detect–Treat–Prevent–Build, Ni-kshay, Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana, notification |
| IDSP | November 2004 | S, P, L forms; rapid response teams; IHIP |
| NLEP | 1955 → NLEP 1983 (MDT); elimination as PHP December 2005 | Case detection, MDT, contact prophylaxis, DPMR |
| NMHP | 1982; DMHP 1996; Tele-MANAS 2022 (14416) | Minimum care for all, integration with general care |
| NPPCD | Pilot 2006–07 (25 districts) | Early detection, hearing aids, training |
| UIP | EPI 1978 → UIP 1985 | Cold chain 2–8 °C, eVIN, Mission Indradhanush, AEFI |
| NPCB&VI | 1976; renamed 2017 | Cataract surgery, school eye screening, eye banks |
| Pulse Polio | 1995; last case January 2011; certified 27 March 2014 | NIDs, house-to-house, AFP surveillance |
| RMNCH+A | 2013; JSY 2005; JSSK June 2011 | Continuum of care, PMSMA, RBSK (4 Ds), RKSK |
| Family planning | 1952 (first in the world) | Basket of choices, rights-based |
| NTCP | 2007–08; COTPA 2003 | Sec 4 public smoking, 5 ads, 6a minors, 6b 100 yards, 7 warnings; quit line 1800-11-2356 |
| Malaria | NMCP 1953 → NMEP 1958 → MPO 1977 → NVBDCP; NFME 2016–2030 | No indigenous transmission by 2027, elimination by 2030 |
| NPHCE | 2010–11 | Geriatric clinics, Regional Geriatric Centres |
| WHO | 1948, Geneva; SEARO New Delhi | IHR 2005, FCTC, DOTS, MDT, polio certification |

**Unit 5 — community services**

| Topic | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| Alma-Ata 1978 | Primary health care; principles: equity, community participation, intersectoral coordination, appropriate technology |
| Norms | SC 5,000/3,000; PHC 30,000/20,000; CHC 1,20,000/80,000 |
| PHC functions | Medical care, MCH, FP, immunisation, disease control, sanitation, health education, school health, lab, records, drugs |
| Rural sanitation | Pour-flush and twin-pit latrines, chlorinated water (residual about 0.5 mg/L after 1 h), soak pits, compost, biogas; SBM (Grameen) 2 October 2014 |
| NUHM | Approved 1 May 2013; towns > 50,000; U-PHC about 1 per 50,000; Mahila Arogya Samiti |

| School health | Appraisal, remedial care, prevention, environment, nutrition, first aid, mental health, education, records |

**Pharmacist's role — one list for every programme answer**

Logistics and cold chain → dispensing and adherence counselling → health education → screening and referral → surveillance and reporting (TB notification, ADR, AEFI) → rational drug use → stigma reduction and confidentiality.

questions.answer:
1. WHO definition (1948): a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity; positive, multidimensional and an ideal.
2. Concepts: biomedical (absence of disease), ecological (balance of agent, host, environment), psychosocial (social, cultural, economic factors), holistic (whole person and community).
3. Dimensions: physical, mental, social, spiritual; also emotional, vocational and environmental.
4. Spectrum of health: positive health → better health → freedom from sickness → unrecognised sickness → mild → severe sickness → death.
5. Determinants: heredity, environment (water, air, housing), lifestyle (diet, exercise, tobacco, alcohol), socio-economic status (income, education, occupation), health services, gender, culture and politics.
6. Indicators: mortality (crude death rate, IMR, MMR, life expectancy), morbidity (incidence, prevalence), disability, nutritional status (low birth weight, stunting), health-care delivery (doctor–population ratio), utilisation (immunisation coverage, institutional deliveries), social and environmental indicators (literacy, safe water, sanitation).
7. Pharmacist links: promotes healthy lifestyle, screening, rational use of medicines.
questions.question: Define health. Explain the changing concepts and dimensions of health, and describe the determinants and indicators of health.

questions.answer:
1. Prevention: actions that stop disease from occurring, detect it early or limit its consequences; based on the natural history of disease (pre-pathogenesis and pathogenesis).
2. Primordial prevention: stop risk factors from appearing in the population — healthy school food, tobacco advertising ban, safe play spaces.
3. Primary prevention (before disease): immunisation, safe water, sanitation, iodised salt, condoms, mosquito nets, health education.
4. Secondary prevention (early disease): screening for hypertension, diabetes, cervical and oral cancer; sputum test for TB; prompt treatment.
5. Tertiary prevention (established disease): disability limitation and rehabilitation — physiotherapy after stroke, leprosy footwear, artificial limbs.
6. Quaternary prevention: protecting patients from over-medicalisation.
7. Modes of intervention (Leavell and Clark): health promotion; specific protection; early diagnosis and treatment; disability limitation; rehabilitation (medical, vocational, social, psychological) — with a table matching each to a level.
8. Control, elimination and eradication defined: control = reduce to acceptable level; elimination = stop transmission in an area or reduce below a set level (leprosy as a public health problem in India); eradication = worldwide end (smallpox).
9. Role of pharmacist at each level: education, vaccines and supplies, screening, adherence, rehabilitation aids.
questions.question: Explain the concept of prevention of disease. Describe the levels of prevention and the modes of intervention with suitable examples.

questions.answer:
1. Malnutrition: undernutrition (deficiency) or overnutrition (obesity); India has a double burden.
2. PEM: marasmus (energy deficiency; no oedema, wasted, old-man face, good appetite) vs kwashiorkor (protein deficiency with infection; oedema, moon face, flag sign hair, flaky-paint skin, fatty liver, poor appetite).
3. Terms: stunting (low height for age), wasting (low weight for height), underweight (low weight for age). SAM (6–59 months): WHZ < −3 SD, MUAC < 115 mm or bilateral pitting oedema.
4. Vitamin deficiencies (table): A — night blindness, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia; D — rickets, osteomalacia; K — bleeding; B1 — beriberi; B2 — angular stomatitis, cheilosis; niacin — pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia); B12 and folate — megaloblastic anaemia, folate deficiency → neural tube defects; C — scurvy.
5. Minerals: iron — anaemia; iodine — goitre and cretinism.
6. Causes: poverty, poor breastfeeding and complementary feeding, infections, large families, ignorance, food taboos, poor sanitation.
7. Prevention: exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months; complementary feeding; growth monitoring; ICDS supplementary nutrition and school meals; fortification (iodised salt, fortified rice); vitamin A, IFA and deworming; immunisation, safe water, sanitation; family planning and women's education; nutrition education.
8. Pharmacist: supplements counselling, referral of malnourished children, nutrition education.
questions.question: What is malnutrition? Describe protein–energy malnutrition and the common vitamin deficiency disorders. Add a note on the prevention of malnutrition.

questions.answer:
1. Balanced diet: a diet containing all nutrients in correct amounts and proportions to meet body needs, with a small margin for lean periods; varies with age, sex, activity and physiological state.
2. Include all food groups: cereals and millets; pulses, eggs, meat, fish; milk and milk products; vegetables and fruits; fats, oils and nuts.
3. Prefer whole grains and millets; combine cereals with pulses (supplementary action of proteins: lysine and methionine).
4. Plenty of colourful vegetables and fruits; adequate water and fibre.
5. Limit sugar, salt, refined, fried and ultra-processed foods; use iodised salt; oils in moderation.
6. Extra needs in pregnancy and lactation (energy, protein, iron, folate, calcium); exclusive breastfeeding for infants to six months.
7. Follow ICMR-NIN dietary guidelines for exact allowances.
questions.question: What is a balanced diet? State the principles of planning a balanced diet.

questions.answer:
1. Urbanisation = movement of people from rural to urban areas and growth of cities.
2. Positive: better access to hospitals and specialists, education, jobs, transport and communication.
3. Negative — environment: slums, overcrowding, poor water supply and drainage, air, noise and water pollution.
4. Communicable diseases: TB, dengue, diarrhoea, HIV spread fast in crowded slums.
5. Non-communicable diseases: sedentary life and fast food → obesity, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease.
6. Injuries: road traffic accidents, industrial accidents.
7. Mental and social: stress, depression, alcohol and drug misuse, crime, loss of joint-family support, isolation of the elderly.
8. Response: NUHM, urban sanitation, town planning, parks, NCD screening.
questions.question: Discuss the impact of urbanisation on health.

questions.answer:
1. Poverty leads to poor nutrition, overcrowded housing, unsafe water and poor sanitation → infections, malnutrition, TB.
2. Low education → less awareness, late care seeking, poor hygiene.
3. Inability to pay → delayed treatment, self-medication, incomplete courses.
4. Illness → loss of wages, cost of treatment, debt (out-of-pocket spending) → deeper poverty.
5. This forms a vicious cycle: poverty → ill health → loss of earnings → poverty (draw the cycle).
6. Breaking the cycle: free primary care, insurance for hospital care (PM-JAY), nutrition programmes, safe water and sanitation, education and employment schemes.
questions.question: Explain the relationship between poverty and health.

questions.answer:
1. Personal hygiene: practices an individual follows to keep the body clean and prevent disease.
2. Components: daily bathing and clean clothes; hand washing with soap before eating and after toilet; care of hair and nails; oral hygiene (brush twice daily); care of eyes, ears and feet (footwear against hookworm); menstrual hygiene; food hygiene; sleep, rest and exercise; respiratory etiquette.
3. Avoidable habits: smoking and chewing tobacco, alcohol misuse, drug abuse, junk food and overeating, sedentary life, self-medication with antibiotics, open defecation and spitting, unsafe sex, excessive screen time.
4. Effects: cancers, heart disease, infections, drug resistance, accidents.
5. Pharmacist: health education, tobacco cessation, safe medicine use.
questions.question: What is personal hygiene? Describe its components and list avoidable habits harmful to health.

questions.answer:
1. Social causes: poverty, illiteracy, overcrowding and slums, unemployment, occupation hazards, harmful customs and beliefs (child marriage, food taboos), gender inequality, addictions.
2. Social problems of the sick: loss of income and job, cost of treatment and debt, stigma and discrimination (TB, leprosy, HIV, mental illness), isolation, broken relationships, interrupted schooling, dependence on family, anxiety and depression.
3. Solutions: health education, free services and insurance, legal protection (HIV/AIDS Act 2017, Mental Healthcare Act 2017), social support, rehabilitation.
4. Pharmacist: kind counselling, confidentiality, guiding patients to free schemes.
questions.question: Describe the social causes of disease and the social problems of the sick.

questions.answer: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity (WHO, 1948).
questions.question: Give the WHO definition of health.

questions.answer: Elimination stops transmission in a defined area or brings a disease below a set level (e.g., leprosy as a public health problem in India); eradication ends the infection worldwide (e.g., smallpox).
questions.question: Differentiate between elimination and eradication.

questions.answer:
1. Agent: Plasmodium falciparum (severe, cerebral malaria), P. vivax (relapses), P. malariae, P. ovale; P. knowlesi occasionally.
2. Vector: female Anopheles, night biting; An. culicifacies (rural), An. stephensi (urban) in India.
3. Life cycle: sexual cycle in mosquito, asexual (liver, then red cell) in humans.
4. Features: fever with chills and rigors, sweating, anaemia, splenomegaly; complications of falciparum — cerebral malaria, severe anaemia, kidney failure, danger in pregnancy.
5. Diagnosis: blood smear (thick and thin) or RDT; test every fever in endemic areas.
6. Treatment principle (national drug policy): ACT for falciparum; chloroquine plus primaquine for vivax (primaquine avoided in pregnancy, infants, G6PD deficiency); parenteral artemisinin derivatives for severe malaria.
7. Prevention and control: early diagnosis and complete treatment; integrated vector management — IRS, LLINs, larvivorous fish (Gambusia, guppy), source reduction, larvicides, fogging in outbreaks; personal protection (nets, repellents, clothing, screens); surveillance; community participation; chemoprophylaxis for some travellers.
8. National programme: NVBDCP/NCVBDC; National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016–2030.
9. Pharmacist: test before treat, full course counselling, G6PD caution, nets and repellents, reporting.
questions.question: Describe the epidemiology, prevention and control of malaria. Add the role of the pharmacist.

questions.answer:
1. Dengue agent: flavivirus with 4 serotypes; second infection with another serotype raises risk of severe dengue.
2. Vector: Aedes aegypti (and A. albopictus), day biting, breeds in clean stored water (coolers, tyres, pots, tanks).
3. Dengue features: high fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, rash; warning signs — abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, restlessness, falling platelets and rising haematocrit; severe dengue = plasma leakage with shock, severe bleeding, organ damage.
4. Diagnosis: NS1 antigen early, IgM later; platelet count and haematocrit.
5. Chikungunya: alphavirus, same Aedes vectors; sudden fever with severe, often prolonged joint pain; rarely fatal; supportive care.
6. Prevention (both): weekly emptying and covering of containers ('dry day'), removing tyres and junk, larvicides, fogging in outbreaks, personal protection by day, nets for patients, community campaigns, National Dengue Day 16 May.
7. Management principle: no specific antiviral; fluids; paracetamol for fever.
8. NSAIDs and aspirin are avoided because they impair platelet function and irritate the stomach, increasing bleeding risk when platelets are low.
9. Pharmacist: fever advice, warning signs, referral, myth-busting.
questions.question: Discuss the epidemiology and prevention of dengue and chikungunya. Why are NSAIDs avoided in dengue?

questions.answer:
1. Definitions: substance abuse — harmful or non-medical use; dependence — craving, loss of control, continued use despite harm, tolerance, withdrawal; psychological vs physical dependence; tolerance; withdrawal.
2. Classification: depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates); opioids (heroin, morphine, codeine cough syrups, tramadol); stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines, nicotine); cannabis; hallucinogens (LSD); inhalants (glue, petrol, whitener); tobacco.
3. Causes: peer pressure, curiosity, stress, family problems, availability, unemployment, mental illness, early tobacco and alcohol use.
4. Effects: organ damage, overdose deaths, HIV and hepatitis from needle sharing, accidents, crime, job loss, family breakdown.
5. Supply reduction: NDPS Act 1985; Schedule H, H1, X controls.
6. Demand reduction: school and college awareness, life skills, family counselling, campaigns.
7. Harm reduction: needle–syringe programmes, opioid substitution therapy.
8. Treatment and rehabilitation: detoxification, de-addiction centres, counselling, self-help groups (AA, NA), vocational rehabilitation, relapse prevention.
9. Pharmacist: dispense controlled drugs only on valid prescription with registers; detect forged or repeat prescriptions; refuse misuse of cough syrups and sedatives; educate; refer; secure storage.
questions.question: Define drug addiction. Classify commonly abused substances and discuss the causes, effects, prevention and control of drug and substance abuse, including the role of the pharmacist.

questions.answer:
1. Agent: Vibrio cholerae O1 (classical, El Tor) and O139.
2. Spread: faecal–oral via contaminated water and food; floods, camps, slums.
3. Incubation: few hours to about 5 days; features: painless rice-water stools, vomiting, rapid dehydration, cramps.
4. Treatment principle: ORS for most, IV fluids for severe dehydration, antibiotics as per guidelines for severe cases, zinc for children.
5. Prevention: safe water (boiling, chlorination), sanitation and latrines, food hygiene, hand washing, disinfection of excreta, notification and outbreak investigation, oral cholera vaccine in high-risk areas, health education.
6. Pharmacist: stock ORS and zinc, teach preparation of ORS, avoid antimotility drugs in children, refer severe cases.
questions.question: Write a note on the prevention and control of cholera.

questions.answer:
1. Agents: Wuchereria bancrofti (most in India), Brugia malayi.
2. Vectors: Culex quinquefasciatus (dirty water) and Mansonia (ponds with water plants).
3. Nocturnal periodicity: night blood smear; antigen tests by day.
4. Features: lymphangitis, lymphoedema, elephantiasis, hydrocele; stigma.
5. Mass drug administration once a year to the eligible population in endemic districts (DEC plus albendazole, or triple-drug with ivermectin in selected districts), taken under supervision.
6. Morbidity management and disability prevention: limb hygiene and exercise; hydrocele surgery.
7. Vector control: drains, larvicides, removing water plants; personal protection.
8. Pharmacist: explain MDA and mild reactions, exclusions (pregnancy, young children, seriously ill).
questions.question: Describe the prevention and control of lymphatic filariasis.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: BP persistently 140/90 mm Hg or more; primary vs secondary.
2. Risk factors: age, family history, obesity, high salt, low potassium, alcohol, tobacco, inactivity, stress, diabetes.
3. Complications: stroke, MI, heart failure, kidney failure, retinopathy; 'silent killer'; rule of halves.
4. Primordial: less salt in processed foods, tobacco control, health education in schools.
5. Primary: salt under 5 g/day (WHO), fruits and vegetables, weight control, exercise, no tobacco, limit alcohol.
6. Secondary: screening of adults, regular antihypertensive treatment and follow-up.
7. Tertiary: stroke and cardiac rehabilitation.
8. Pharmacist: BP checks, adherence counselling, lifestyle advice, avoid NSAIDs/decongestants without advice.
questions.question: Discuss the prevention and control of hypertension.

questions.answer:
1. Common cancers in India: oral, lung, breast, cervical.
2. Risk factors: tobacco (largest preventable), alcohol, HPV, hepatitis B and C, H. pylori, obesity, inactivity, radiation, occupational carcinogens, air pollution, heredity.
3. Warning signs — CAUTION: change in bowel/bladder habits, a sore that does not heal, unusual bleeding, thickening or lump, indigestion or difficulty swallowing, obvious change in wart or mole, nagging cough or hoarseness.
4. Primary prevention: tobacco and alcohol control, diet and exercise, HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, safe sex, workplace protection.
5. Secondary: screening — oral visual examination, clinical breast examination, VIA/Pap/HPV test for cervix; early treatment.
6. Tertiary: surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, palliative care.
7. Pharmacist: tobacco cessation, awareness, chemotherapy counselling, palliative care.
questions.question: Write a note on the prevention and early detection of cancer.

questions.answer:
1. ARI: upper (cold, pharyngitis, otitis) and lower (bronchiolitis, pneumonia); major cause of under-five deaths.
2. Agents: RSV, influenza, measles; S. pneumoniae, Hib, S. aureus.
3. Risk factors: low birth weight, malnutrition, no breastfeeding, overcrowding, indoor smoke, parental smoking, missed vaccines, vitamin A deficiency.
4. Fast breathing cut-offs: < 2 months ≥ 60, 2–12 months ≥ 50, 1–5 years ≥ 40 per minute; chest indrawing and danger signs → urgent referral.
5. Prevention: vaccines (measles, pertussis, Hib, PCV), exclusive breastfeeding, nutrition and vitamin A, clean fuel and ventilation, hand washing, less crowding.
6. Case management with antibiotics by trained workers per national protocol; oxygen for severe cases.
7. Pharmacist: no antibiotics for simple cold, recognise danger signs, ensure complete course.
questions.question: Explain the prevention and control of acute respiratory infections and pneumonia in children.

questions.answer: Drift is small, gradual change in the haemagglutinin or neuraminidase antigens causing seasonal epidemics; shift is a sudden major change producing a new subtype that can cause a pandemic.
questions.question: What is antigenic drift and antigenic shift in influenza?

questions.answer: Malaria — female Anopheles; dengue — Aedes aegypti (and A. albopictus); bancroftian filariasis — Culex quinquefasciatus.
questions.question: Name the vectors of malaria, dengue and bancroftian filariasis.

questions.answer:
1. Background: run by NACO (set up 1992) with State AIDS Control Societies; implemented in phases; phase V from April 2021 to March 2026.
2. Objectives: sharply reduce new infections and AIDS-related deaths (80% reduction from 2010 levels as stated aim), eliminate vertical transmission of HIV and syphilis, reach 95-95-95, reduce stigma.
3. Targeted interventions for high-risk groups: condoms, STI care, counselling; harm reduction — needle–syringe exchange and opioid substitution therapy.
4. ICTC: free confidential counselling and testing.
5. PPTCT: testing all pregnant women, lifelong ART for positive mothers, infant prophylaxis and testing.
6. ART and Link ART centres: free lifelong treatment, viral load monitoring, opportunistic infection care.
7. STI/RTI clinics (Suraksha clinics), blood safety, IEC (Red Ribbon Clubs), helpline, surveillance.
8. Legal: HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 — non-discrimination, consent and confidentiality.
9. Outcome: low adult prevalence, falling new infections and deaths, wide free ART coverage; gaps in testing and viral load coverage.
10. Pharmacist: discreet condom/syringe supply, referral for testing, ART adherence counselling, side effects and interactions, PEP awareness, confidentiality, fight stigma.
questions.question: Describe the objectives, functioning and outcome of the National AIDS Control Programme. Add the role of the pharmacist.

questions.answer:
1. Background: RNTCP started 1997 (pilot 1993) with DOTS; renamed NTEP in January 2020; National Strategic Plan 2017–2025 aimed to end TB ahead of the global 2030 target (check current plan on tbcindia.mohfw.gov.in).
2. Objectives: reduce incidence and deaths; no catastrophic costs; find all cases including private sector.
3. Detect: test presumptive TB (cough ≥ 2 weeks); CBNAAT/Truenat, microscopy, chest X-ray; active case finding; mandatory notification by doctors, labs and chemists.
4. Treat: free daily fixed-dose combinations; shorter regimens for drug-resistant TB; treatment supporters; adherence technology; Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (nutrition support via DBT).
5. Prevent: TB preventive therapy for contacts and PLHIV; BCG; airborne infection control.
6. Build: Ni-kshay online system; private sector engagement; Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan with Ni-kshay Mitras.
7. Outcome: higher notification, wider molecular testing, fall in incidence and deaths; TB still a major problem.
8. Pharmacist: refer coughers, treatment supporter, adherence and side effects (red urine with rifampicin; report jaundice), record anti-TB drug sales and notify, World TB Day (24 March).
questions.question: Discuss the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme with respect to its objectives, strategies and outcome.

questions.answer:
1. UIP background: EPI 1978 → UIP 1985; part of NHM; Mission Indradhanush catch-up drives; eVIN for stock and cold-chain monitoring.
2. UIP objectives: high coverage, quality services, reliable cold chain, district-wise monitoring, vaccine self-sufficiency.
3. Main vaccines: Td in pregnancy; BCG, OPV-0 and hepatitis B at birth; OPV, pentavalent, rotavirus, fIPV, PCV in infancy; MR, JE (endemic areas) and boosters later; Td at 10 and 16 years (check current schedule on mohfw.gov.in).
4. Functioning: fixed-day sessions at sub-centres and Anganwadis, ASHA mobilisation, cold chain, vaccine vial monitors, AEFI surveillance.
5. Pulse Polio: launched 1995; national and sub-national immunisation days giving OPV to all under-fives on the same day; booth plus house-to-house; transit and mobile teams; finger and house marking; AFP surveillance (under 15 years) and sewage surveillance.
6. Outcome: last wild polio case January 2011; WHO certified India (SEAR) polio-free on 27 March 2014; maternal and neonatal tetanus eliminated; coverage rising; new vaccines added.
7. Pharmacist: cold chain 2–8 °C, no freezing of DPT/HepB/Td/PCV, VVM and expiry checks, reminders, AEFI reporting, myth busting.
questions.question: Describe the Universal Immunization Programme and the Pulse Polio programme. What has been their outcome?

questions.answer:
1. Launched November 2004 with World Bank assistance; now under NHM; reporting on the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP).
2. Objective: decentralised, lab-based, IT-enabled surveillance of epidemic-prone diseases to detect outbreaks early and respond rapidly.
3. Reporting forms: S (syndromic, by health workers), P (presumptive, by medical officers), L (laboratory-confirmed).
4. Weekly reporting plus immediate reporting of unusual events; surveillance units at centre, state, district.
5. Rapid response teams investigate outbreaks; referral lab network; media scanning.
6. Diseases include diarrhoea/cholera, typhoid, hepatitis, malaria, dengue, measles, AES, ILI.
7. Pharmacist: report unusual rise in sales of ORS, antipyretics, antimalarials; outbreak supply.
questions.question: Write a note on the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP).

questions.answer:
1. Background: control programme 1955 (dapsone) → NLEP 1983 with MDT; elimination as public health problem (< 1 per 10,000) nationally in December 2005.
2. Objectives: reduce burden, interrupt transmission, prevent grade 2 disabilities, reduce stigma.
3. Case detection campaigns (house-to-house), contact examination, Sparsh awareness campaign.
4. Free MDT blister packs for PB and MB leprosy.
5. Single-dose rifampicin post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts.
6. DPMR: self-care, MCR footwear, reconstructive surgery; social rehabilitation.
7. Outcome: big fall in prevalence; new cases still detected.
8. Pharmacist: recognise anaesthetic patches, MDT counselling (red urine, skin darkening), recognise reactions, fight stigma.
questions.question: Describe the National Leprosy Eradication Programme.

questions.answer:
1. Launched 1982; DMHP 1996 (Bellary model); Tele-MANAS launched 10 October 2022 (toll-free 14416); Mental Healthcare Act 2017.
2. Objectives: minimum mental health care for all, especially the vulnerable; integrate mental health with general care and social development; community participation.
3. DMHP: early detection and treatment, training of general doctors and workers, IEC, records.
4. Tertiary strengthening, Centres of Excellence, manpower training.
5. Life-skills, school mental health, suicide prevention, workplace stress.
6. Primary-care screening at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
7. Pharmacist: recognise depression/suicide risk and refer, adherence (do not stop antidepressants suddenly), safe storage, reduce stigma.
questions.question: Write a note on the National Mental Health Programme.

questions.answer:
1. Launched 1976 (Trachoma Control Programme of 1963 merged); renamed NPCB&VI in 2017 to cover all visual impairment.
2. Goal stated by the government: reduce avoidable blindness prevalence to 0.25% by 2025 (check current target).
3. Causes: cataract (leading), refractive errors, glaucoma, corneal blindness, diabetic retinopathy, childhood blindness.
4. Activities: free cataract surgery with IOL; school eye screening and free spectacles; spectacles for presbyopia; eye banks and keratoplasty; glaucoma and DR care; vision centres; training; NGO support; Eye Donation Fortnight.
5. Pharmacist: eye checks for diabetics, correct eye-drop use, avoid steroid drops without prescription, promote eye donation.
questions.question: Write a note on the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment.

questions.answer:
1. Started as a pilot in 2006–07 (January 2007) in 25 districts; expanded in phases.
2. Objectives: prevent avoidable hearing loss from disease or injury; early identification, diagnosis and treatment of ear problems; medical rehabilitation of deaf persons of all ages; build institutional capacity for ear care.
3. Activities: training of ENT staff and audiologists; equipment at district hospitals; newborn and school screening; free hearing aids and speech therapy; IEC.
4. Preventable causes: chronic ear infections, wax, noise, ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides), measles, mumps, meningitis, rubella in pregnancy, birth asphyxia, neonatal jaundice.
5. Pharmacist: avoid self-medication in discharging ears, warn about ototoxic drugs, advise ear protection, refer children with poor speech.
questions.question: Write a note on the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Deafness.

questions.answer: S = syndromic reporting by health workers; P = presumptive (clinical) diagnosis by medical officers; L = laboratory-confirmed cases reported by labs.
questions.question: What are the S, P and L forms of IDSP?

questions.answer: India (with the WHO South-East Asia Region) was certified polio-free on 27 March 2014; AFP surveillance reports and tests every case of acute flaccid paralysis in children under 15 years to detect any poliovirus.
questions.question: When was India certified polio-free, and what is AFP surveillance?

questions.answer:
1. Background: RCH approach; RMNCH+A strategy adopted in 2013 for the continuum of care (adolescence → pregnancy → delivery → newborn → childhood); nutrition component added later; runs under NHM.
2. Objectives: reduce MMR, IMR, NMR and under-five mortality; reduce TFR; improve adolescent health and anaemia.
3. Reproductive: spacing and permanent methods, home delivery of contraceptives by ASHA, post-partum family planning.
4. Maternal: JSY (12 April 2005) — cash incentive for institutional delivery for poor women; JSSK (June 2011) — free delivery including caesarean, drugs, tests, diet, blood and transport; PMSMA — free specialist ANC on a fixed day each month; four ANC visits, IFA, calcium, Td, high-risk identification.
5. Newborn: essential newborn care, breastfeeding within one hour, newborn care corners, SNCUs, home-based newborn care, kangaroo mother care.
6. Child: UIP, exclusive breastfeeding, ORS–zinc, pneumonia management, vitamin A, deworming, RBSK (4 Ds), nutrition rehabilitation centres.
7. Adolescent: RKSK — nutrition, SRH, mental health, injuries, substance misuse, NCDs; adolescent-friendly clinics; WIFS; menstrual hygiene.
8. Cross-cutting: Anemia Mukt Bharat, death reviews, MCP card, ASHA incentives.
9. Outcome: rise in institutional deliveries, marked fall in MMR, IMR, U5MR; anaemia and stunting remain.
10. Pharmacist: IFA/calcium/ORS–zinc counselling, danger signs, safe drugs in pregnancy, contraception advice.
questions.question: Describe the national health intervention programme for mother and child (RMNCH+A) with its major schemes.

questions.answer:
1. NMCP 1953 — IRS with DDT; large fall in cases.
2. NMEP 1958 — eradication attempt.
3. Resurgence in the 1970s — insecticide and drug resistance, operational and financial problems.
4. Modified Plan of Operation 1977, with P. falciparum containment — aim to prevent deaths and reduce morbidity.
5. Early 2000s — integrated into NVBDCP covering malaria, dengue, chikungunya, filariasis, JE, kala-azar; now run by NCVBDC.
6. National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016–2030: interrupt indigenous transmission in all states/UTs by 2027; zero indigenous cases nationally by 2030; National Strategic Plan 2023–2027.
7. Strategy: early diagnosis (RDT, microscopy by ASHAs) and complete treatment (ACT for Pf, CQ + PQ for Pv); IRS, LLINs, larvivorous fish, source reduction; case-based surveillance and district stratification (categories 0–3); BCC; intersectoral work; drug efficacy monitoring.
8. Outcome: sharp fall in cases and deaths since 2015; residual burden in forest and tribal areas.
9. Pharmacist: test before treat, full course, G6PD caution, nets and repellents, reporting.
questions.question: Trace the history of malaria control in India and describe the current strategy for malaria elimination.

questions.answer:
1. Background: NTCP launched 2007–08 in 42 districts of 21 states/UTs; now in all states and UTs; India is a party to WHO FCTC.
2. Objectives: awareness of harmful effects; reduce production and supply; implement COTPA 2003; help people quit; implement FCTC strategies.
3. COTPA sections: 4 — no smoking in public places; 5 — ban on direct/indirect advertising and sponsorship; 6(a) — no sale to or by persons under 18; 6(b) — no sale within 100 yards of educational institutions; 7 — specified (pictorial) health warnings.
4. Functioning: national, state and district tobacco control cells; tobacco cessation centres; national quit line 1800-11-2356; training of health workers, police and teachers; tobacco-free educational institutions; enforcement squads; mass media; World No Tobacco Day 31 May; e-cigarette ban (2019 Act).
5. Outcome: fall in adult tobacco use, but smokeless tobacco and oral cancer remain major problems.
6. Pharmacist: 5 A's (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange); 5 R's for unwilling (Relevance, Risks, Rewards, Roadblocks, Repetition); nicotine replacement therapy counselling; referral to quit line and cessation centres; not selling tobacco.
questions.question: Describe the National Tobacco Control Programme and the main provisions of COTPA, 2003. Discuss the role of the pharmacist in tobacco cessation.

questions.answer:
1. India was the first country to start a national family planning programme (1952, First Five Year Plan); later broadened to family welfare and a target-free, rights-based approach; National Population Policy 2000.
2. Objectives: meet unmet need, stabilise population, improve maternal and child health through spacing.
3. Spacing methods: condoms, combined oral pills, centchroman, injectable MPA, copper IUCD (including post-partum), emergency contraceptive pill.
4. Permanent methods: tubectomy (laparoscopic, mini-lap), vasectomy (including no-scalpel).
5. Support: home delivery by ASHA, compensation for sterilisation, indemnity scheme, Mission Parivar Vikas in high-fertility districts, safe abortion under MTP Act, logistics system, IEC.
6. Outcome: TFR near replacement nationally; low male participation.
7. Pharmacist: counselling on choice and correct use, missed pills, emergency contraception, dual protection.
questions.question: Write a note on the National Family Welfare Programme and the methods of contraception.

questions.answer:
1. Launched 2010–11 by MoHFW for people aged 60 and above; under NCD flexible pool of NHM.
2. Objectives: accessible promotive, preventive, curative and rehabilitative care through community-based primary care; identify and manage elderly health problems; capacity building of staff and family carers; referral services.
3. Services: sub-centre/Ayushman Arogya Mandir — education, home visits; PHC and CHC — geriatric clinics, physiotherapy; district hospital — geriatric OPD and ward; Regional Geriatric Centres in medical colleges; National Centres for Ageing.
4. Common problems: hypertension, diabetes, arthritis and falls, cataract, deafness, dementia, depression, polypharmacy.
5. Pharmacist: medication review, reduce polypharmacy, pill organisers, large labels, fall-risk drug counselling, vaccination awareness.
questions.question: Write a note on the National Programme for the Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE).

questions.answer:
1. WHO: UN health agency, founded 1948, HQ Geneva; India in South-East Asia Region with regional office in New Delhi; country office for India.
2. General functions: norms and standards (essential medicines list, ICD, guidelines), technical cooperation, epidemic surveillance under IHR (2005), research and statistics, prequalification.
3. Smallpox eradication; polio — National Polio Surveillance Project and certification (2014).
4. TB — DOTS and End TB strategy; leprosy — MDT recommended and supplied free for many years.
5. Malaria and vector-borne diseases — technical strategy and drug policy; HIV and hepatitis guidelines.
6. NCDs and tobacco — action plans, FCTC; mental health — mhGAP; blindness initiative.
7. Emergencies — SARS, Ebola, influenza, COVID-19 response; medicines — essential medicines concept for NLEM, pharmacovigilance, GMP.
questions.question: Describe the role of WHO in Indian national health programmes.

questions.answer:
1. Social health programmes: the community-based arm of health programmes using community workers, other sectors and social support.
2. ASHA under NHM: village health activist; mobilises for immunisation and institutional delivery, newborn visits, depot holder for ORS, contraceptives, IFA.
3. VHSNC and Village Health and Nutrition Days: community planning, monthly service day.
4. ICDS/POSHAN Abhiyaan: supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring, pre-school education via Anganwadi.
5. School meals (PM POSHAN).
6. Ayushman Bharat: Ayushman Arogya Mandirs and PM-JAY insurance.
7. Jan Aushadhi Kendras: low-cost generics run by pharmacists.
8. Swachh Bharat Mission; Rogi Kalyan Samitis.
9. Pharmacist: work with ASHAs, camps, Jan Aushadhi, guiding people to schemes.
questions.question: What is meant by social health programmes? Give examples of community-based schemes that support health in India.

questions.answer:
1. Janani Suraksha Yojana (launched 12 April 2005): conditional cash transfer to promote institutional delivery among poor pregnant women; ASHA as link worker; aims to reduce maternal and neonatal deaths.
2. Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (June 2011): free delivery including caesarean section in public facilities, free drugs, diagnostics, diet, blood, and transport (home to facility, referral, drop back) for pregnant women and sick infants.
3. Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram: child health screening from birth to 18 years for the 4 Ds — defects at birth, deficiencies, diseases, developmental delays — by mobile health teams in Anganwadis and schools, with referral to District Early Intervention Centres for free treatment.
4. All three work under RMNCH+A of NHM.

questions.answer: Ask about tobacco use, Advise to quit, Assess willingness, Assist in quitting (counselling, NRT), Arrange follow-up.
questions.question: State the 5 A's of tobacco cessation.

questions.answer: Interrupt indigenous transmission of malaria in all states and UTs by 2027 and achieve zero indigenous cases (elimination) in the whole country by 2030.
questions.question: What are the elimination goals of the National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016–2030?

questions.answer:
1. Definition (Alma-Ata 1978): essential health care based on practical, scientifically sound and socially acceptable methods, universally accessible to individuals and families through full participation, at affordable cost; first level of contact.
2. Principles: equitable distribution, community participation, intersectoral coordination, appropriate technology, emphasis on prevention.
3. Elements (ELEMENTS): education on health problems; locally endemic disease control; expanded immunisation; maternal and child health with family planning; essential drugs; nutrition; treatment of common illness; safe water and sanitation.
4. Rural set-up and norms: sub-centre 5,000/3,000; PHC 30,000/20,000; CHC 1,20,000/80,000; Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
5. PHC functions: medical care and referral; MCH; family planning; immunisation; control of communicable diseases; NCD screening; environmental sanitation and safe water; health education; school health; basic lab; vital statistics and records; supervision and training; national programmes; free drugs.
6. Staff: medical officer, pharmacist, nurses, LHV, health assistants, lab technician.
7. Pharmacist at PHC: indenting, storage, cold chain, dispensing and counselling, records, programme drugs, health education, ADR reporting.
questions.question: Define primary health care. Describe its principles and elements, and the functions of a Primary Health Centre in India.

questions.answer:
1. Background: approved by the Union Cabinet on 1 May 2013 as a sub-mission of NHM; covers cities and towns above 50,000 population and district/state headquarters.
2. Need: rapid urbanisation, slums, poor water and sanitation, worse indicators among urban poor, lack of public primary care, NCD/TB/vector-borne burden.
3. Objectives: essential primary care for the urban poor, reduce out-of-pocket spending, strengthen public health systems in cities, partner with ULBs, NGOs and private sector.
4. Vulnerable groups: slum dwellers, homeless, rag pickers, street children, rickshaw pullers, construction and brick-kiln workers, sex workers, migrants.
5. Community level: urban ASHA; Mahila Arogya Samiti with untied fund.
6. Outreach: urban health and nutrition days, special camps, mobile units.
7. U-PHC: about one per 50,000 population, in or near slums, convenient OPD hours, free drugs and tests, immunisation, FP, NCD screening (urban Ayushman Arogya Mandirs).
8. U-CHC and district hospitals for referral; convergence with sanitation, ICDS, housing and livelihood schemes.
9. Outcome and gaps; pharmacist's role in dispensing, counselling, screening and Jan Aushadhi.
questions.question: Describe the National Urban Health Mission — its need, objectives, structure and functioning.

questions.answer:
1. Importance: large population group, habit-forming age, carry messages home, early detection of correctable problems.
2. Objectives: promote positive health, prevent disease, detect and correct defects early, provide a healthy environment, create awareness among children, parents and teachers.
3. Health appraisal: periodic examination (height, weight, vision, hearing, teeth, anaemia, skin) and daily observation by teachers.
4. Remedial measures and follow-up: treatment, spectacles, dental care, referral.
5. Prevention of communicable diseases: immunisation checks, Td, isolation, deworming.
6. Healthful environment: site, classrooms, light, ventilation, safe water, separate toilets, hand washing, waste disposal, playground.
7. Nutritional services: PM POSHAN school meal, WIFS, nutrition education.
8. First aid and emergency care; mental health and life skills; dental, eye, ear care.
9. Health education: hygiene, hand washing, menstrual hygiene, road safety, substance abuse, age-appropriate SRH; inclusive education; school health records.
10. Programmes: RBSK screening, School Health and Wellness Programme (health and wellness ambassadors), National Deworming Day, tobacco-free schools.
11. Pharmacist: talks on hygiene and safe medicine use, anti-tobacco and anti-drug education, first-aid kits and training, support for deworming and IFA days.
questions.question: What are school health services? Describe their objectives and components, and the role of the pharmacist in school health promotion.

questions.answer:
1. Problems: open defecation, unsafe water, poor drainage, cattle near houses, refuse heaps, flies and mosquitoes.
2. Excreta disposal: household sanitary latrines — pour-flush water-seal, twin-pit, septic tank; community and school toilets.
3. Safe water: protected wells with parapet and cover, hand pumps, piped supply; chlorination with bleaching powder to leave about 0.5 mg/L free residual chlorine after one hour; household boiling, chlorine tablets, filtration.
4. Sullage: soak pits, kitchen gardens, covered drains.
5. Solid waste: segregation, compost pits, vermicompost, biogas from dung.
6. Housing: ventilation, separate cattle sheds, clean cooking fuel.
7. Vector control: remove stagnant water, drainage.
8. Programmes: Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen) from 2 October 2014 — ODF and ODF Plus; Jal Jeevan Mission; VHSNC funds.
9. Benefits: fewer diarrhoeal diseases, typhoid, hepatitis A/E, worms; less stunting; dignity for women.
questions.question: Describe the measures for improvement of rural sanitation.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a process that informs, motivates and helps people adopt and maintain healthy practices; aims at changes in knowledge, attitude and practice.
2. Principles: interest (felt needs), participation, known to unknown, comprehension (local language), reinforcement, motivation, learning by doing, credibility, good human relations, use of leaders; 'soil, seed and sower'.
3. Individual methods: counselling, home visits, pharmacy counter advice.
4. Group methods: lecture, demonstration, group discussion, panel, symposium, role play, workshop.
5. Mass methods: TV, radio, newspapers, posters, social media, exhibitions, street plays.
6. Communication process: source → message → channel → receiver → feedback; barriers (language, literacy, beliefs, noise, mistrust).
7. Pharmacist as health educator on health days and at the counter.
questions.question: What is health education? Describe its principles and methods.

questions.answer:
1. Health promotion (Ottawa Charter, 1986): enabling people to increase control over, and improve, their health.
2. Build healthy public policy — tobacco taxes, smoke-free laws, food labelling.
3. Create supportive environments — safe water, parks, healthy canteens.
4. Strengthen community action — VHSNC, Mahila Arogya Samiti.
5. Develop personal skills — health education, life skills.
6. Reorient health services towards prevention and promotion.
7. Strategies: advocate, enable, mediate.
8. Examples in India: COTPA, Swachh Bharat, school health and wellness programme, Ayushman Arogya Mandir wellness activities.
questions.question: Explain the concept of health promotion with reference to the Ottawa Charter.

questions.answer:
1. Three-tier primary care network under NHM linked to district hospitals.
2. Village: ASHA, Anganwadi worker, VHSNC.
3. Sub-centre: ANM and multipurpose worker; 5,000 population (3,000 in hilly/tribal); many upgraded to Ayushman Arogya Mandirs with a community health officer.
4. PHC: medical officer and team; 30,000 (20,000); about six beds; referral unit for sub-centres.
5. CHC: 1,20,000 (80,000); 30 beds with physician, surgeon, obstetrician and paediatrician; first referral unit for about four PHCs.
6. District hospital: secondary care.

# Unit 1: Concept of Health and Disease, Nutrition, Sociology and Hygiene

This unit lays the base for the whole subject. It answers four questions: **What is health? What causes disease and how do we prevent it? How does food affect health? How do society, poverty, cities and personal habits affect health?** Almost every later unit (diseases, national programmes, community services) builds on these ideas.

## 1.1 Concept of health

**WHO definition (1948):** "Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity."

Points to note when you explain the definition:

- It is **positive**: health is more than "no disease".
- It is **multidimensional**: body, mind and social life all count.
- It is an **ideal**: "complete" well-being is hard to reach, so it is better seen as a goal.
- A fourth dimension, **spiritual health**, is often added. Many textbooks also mention emotional, vocational and environmental dimensions.

**Changing concepts of health**

| Concept | Main idea | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Biomedical | Health = absence of disease; disease is caused by germs or body faults | Ignores mind, society and environment |
| Ecological | Health = balance between person and environment (agent, host, environment) | Hard to measure |
| Psychosocial | Social, psychological, cultural and economic factors shape health | Can underplay biology |
| Holistic | Combines all the above; looks at the whole person and the community | Broad, needs many sectors to work together |

**Dimensions of health**

1. **Physical** — organs work normally; normal pulse, BP, weight, sleep, appetite.
2. **Mental** — free from mental illness, able to cope with stress, think clearly, work productively.
3. **Social** — good relations with family and society; able to fit into a community.
4. **Spiritual** — sense of purpose, values and inner peace.
5. **Emotional, vocational, environmental** — feeling in control of emotions, satisfaction from work, a safe surrounding.

**Spectrum of health:** health and disease are not two boxes but a continuous line.

```text
Positive health → Better health → Freedom from sickness → Unrecognised sickness → Mild sickness → Severe sickness → Death
```

**Determinants of health:** heredity (genes), environment (water, air, housing), lifestyle (diet, exercise, tobacco, alcohol), socio-economic conditions (income, education, occupation), health services (availability, quality, cost), and other factors (gender, culture, politics).

**Indicators of health** (how we measure the health of a community): mortality indicators (crude death rate, infant mortality rate, maternal mortality ratio, life expectancy), morbidity indicators (incidence, prevalence), disability rates, nutritional status (low birth weight, stunting), health-care delivery (doctor–population ratio), utilisation (immunisation coverage, institutional deliveries), social and economic indicators (literacy, income), environmental indicators (safe water, sanitation).

## 1.2 Concept of disease

**Disease** is a departure from normal structure or function that produces signs and symptoms. Three related words:

- **Disease** — the biological abnormality (doctor's view).
- **Illness** — how the person feels about being unwell (patient's view).
- **Sickness** — the social role of being unwell (society's view; e.g., leave from work).

**Epidemiological triad**

```text
            AGENT
     (germ, chemical, deficiency)
           /      \
          /        \
       HOST ------ ENVIRONMENT
 (age, sex, immunity,   (physical, biological,
  genes, habits)          social)
```

Disease results when the balance among agent, host and environment is disturbed. Prevention aims to restore that balance (kill the agent, protect the host, improve the environment).

**Multifactorial causation** applies to non-communicable diseases such as coronary heart disease: smoking, diet, obesity, high BP, stress, lack of exercise and genes all act together. There is no single "agent".

**Natural history of disease** has two periods:

```text
PRE-PATHOGENESIS (before the person is affected)      PATHOGENESIS (inside the host)
Agent, host and environment interact      →   Early changes → Signs and symptoms → Recovery / Disability / Death
```

**Iceberg of disease:** the cases seen in hospitals are only the tip. Below the surface lie undiagnosed, mild and carrier cases. Screening and surveillance try to find this hidden part (for example, undiagnosed diabetes and hypertension).

## 1.3 Public health and its evolution

**Public health** (Winslow's idea, in short): the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health through the organised efforts of society.

**How public health developed ("evolution of public health")**

| Phase | Key events |
| --- | --- |
| Ancient | Indus valley drains and baths; Ayurveda's rules on diet and daily routine; Hippocrates linked disease with air, water and place |
| Disease-control phase | John Snow linked cholera to a contaminated water pump in London (1854); sanitation reforms in England |
| Germ theory | Pasteur and Koch proved that microbes cause disease; vaccines developed (Jenner's smallpox vaccination, 1796) |
| Health-promotion phase | Focus on lifestyle and behaviour; Alma-Ata Declaration on primary health care (1978); Ottawa Charter for health promotion (1986) |
| Modern | Global goals (Sustainable Development Goals), universal health coverage, surveillance for new infections |

**"Evaluation of public health"** in the syllabus can be answered by describing how public health action is judged: by health indicators (falling IMR and MMR, rising life expectancy), by coverage (immunisation, safe water, institutional delivery), by programme outcomes (polio eliminated, leprosy eliminated as a public health problem) and by equity (whether the poor benefit).

## 1.4 Prevention and control of disease

**Levels of prevention**

| Level | Stage of disease | Aim | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Primordial | Before risk factors appear | Stop risk factors from arising in a population | Healthy school food, ban on tobacco advertising, safe play areas |
| Primary | Risk factors present, no disease | Prevent the disease | Immunisation, safe water, condoms, mosquito nets, iodised salt |
| Secondary | Early disease | Early diagnosis and prompt treatment | Screening for BP, diabetes, cervical cancer; sputum test for TB |
| Tertiary | Established disease | Limit disability, rehabilitate | Physiotherapy after stroke, artificial limbs, leprosy footwear |

Some books add **quaternary prevention**: protecting patients from over-medicalisation and unnecessary tests or drugs.

**Modes of intervention (Leavell and Clark)**

1. Health promotion — health education, nutrition, housing, lifestyle change.
2. Specific protection — vaccines, chemoprophylaxis, protection against occupational hazards.
3. Early diagnosis and treatment — screening, case finding.
4. Disability limitation — complete treatment to stop complications.
5. Rehabilitation — medical, vocational, social and psychological.

**Control, elimination and eradication**

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control | Reduce incidence or prevalence to a level where it is no longer a major problem | Malaria control |
| Elimination | Stop transmission in a defined area, or reduce below a set level ("as a public health problem") | Leprosy eliminated as a public health problem in India |
| Eradication | Remove the infection worldwide; no more cases anywhere | Smallpox |

## 1.5 Social causes of disease and social problems of the sick

**Social causes of disease**

- **Poverty** — poor food, overcrowded housing, no safe water.
- **Illiteracy** — less awareness of hygiene, late care seeking.
- **Overcrowding and slums** — spread of TB, respiratory and skin infections.
- **Unemployment** — stress, depression, alcohol misuse.
- **Occupation** — dust diseases, injuries, pesticide exposure.
- **Customs and beliefs** — child marriage, food taboos in pregnancy, belief that illness is a curse.
- **Gender inequality** — girls fed last, less care for women.
- **Addictions** — tobacco, alcohol, drugs.

**Social problems of the sick person**

- Loss of income, cost of treatment, debt (out-of-pocket spending).
- Stigma and discrimination (TB, leprosy, HIV, mental illness).
- Isolation, broken relationships, divorce.
- Loss of job or schooling.
- Dependence on others; burden on family carers.
- Psychological problems: fear, anxiety, depression.

The pharmacist helps by kind counselling, keeping confidentiality, guiding patients to free government schemes and support groups, and fighting myths.

## 1.6 Food in relation to nutrition and health

**Nutrition** is the science of food, its nutrients and their use by the body for growth, repair and energy.

| Nutrient group | Main role | Sources |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carbohydrates | Main energy source | Cereals, millets, potatoes, sugar |
| Proteins | Growth and repair, enzymes, antibodies | Pulses, milk, eggs, meat, fish, soya |
| Fats | Concentrated energy, fat-soluble vitamins, essential fatty acids | Oils, ghee, nuts, seeds |
| Vitamins | Regulate body processes | Fruits, vegetables, milk, liver |
| Minerals | Bones, blood, nerve and muscle function | Milk (calcium), green leaves and jaggery (iron), iodised salt |
| Water | Medium for all body reactions, temperature control | Drinking water, food |
| Dietary fibre | Bowel movement, lowers cholesterol and blood sugar rise | Whole grains, vegetables, fruits |

**Energy values:** carbohydrate and protein about 4 kcal per gram; fat about 9 kcal per gram.

**Quality of protein:** cereals are low in lysine, pulses are low in methionine. Eating them together (dal-rice, khichdi) gives a better protein mix — the **supplementary action** of proteins.

## 1.7 Balanced diet

A **balanced diet** contains all nutrients in the right amounts and proportions to meet the body's needs, with a small extra for lean periods. It depends on age, sex, body weight, activity and physiological state (pregnancy, lactation).

**Principles**

- Include foods from all groups: cereals and millets; pulses, eggs, meat, fish; milk and milk products; vegetables and fruits; oils, fats and nuts.
- Prefer whole grains and millets; plenty of vegetables and fruits of different colours.
- Limit sugar, salt, refined foods, fried and ultra-processed foods.
- Use iodised salt; use oils in moderation and vary them.
- Drink safe water; be physically active.

> The National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) publishes the Recommended Dietary Allowances and Dietary Guidelines for Indians. Check the latest edition for exact amounts.

**Special groups:** pregnant and lactating women need extra energy, protein, iron, folic acid and calcium; infants need exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, then complementary foods with continued breastfeeding; elderly need soft, fibre-rich, protein-adequate food with calcium and vitamin D.

## 1.8 Nutritional and vitamin deficiencies

**Vitamin deficiency diseases**

| Vitamin | Deficiency disease / signs |
| --- | --- |
| A (retinol) | Night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia (can cause blindness), poor immunity |
| D | Rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults |
| E | Nerve problems, haemolysis in premature infants |
| K | Bleeding tendency (haemorrhagic disease of the newborn) |
| B1 (thiamine) | Beriberi (dry, wet), Wernicke's encephalopathy in alcoholics |
| B2 (riboflavin) | Angular stomatitis, cheilosis, glossitis |
| B3 (niacin) | Pellagra: dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia (death) |
| B6 (pyridoxine) | Peripheral neuropathy, convulsions in infants (may follow isoniazid use) |
| B12 | Megaloblastic anaemia, nerve damage |
| Folic acid | Megaloblastic anaemia; neural tube defects in the baby |
| C | Scurvy: bleeding gums, poor wound healing |

**Mineral deficiencies**

| Mineral | Deficiency |
| --- | --- |
| Iron | Iron-deficiency anaemia (fatigue, pallor, low work capacity, low birth weight) |
| Iodine | Goitre, cretinism, mental retardation, stillbirths — iodine deficiency disorders |
| Calcium | Poor bone growth, osteoporosis |
| Zinc | Poor growth, delayed wound healing, diarrhoea |
| Fluoride | Too little → dental caries; too much → fluorosis |

## 1.9 Malnutrition and its prevention

**Malnutrition** means either **undernutrition** (deficiency) or **overnutrition** (obesity, excess). India faces a "double burden" — undernutrition in children and women, and rising obesity and diabetes.

**Protein–energy malnutrition (PEM)**

| Feature | Marasmus | Kwashiorkor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main deficiency | Energy (and protein) | Mainly protein, with infection |
| Oedema | Absent | Present |
| Look | "Skin and bones", old man face | Moon face, puffy |
| Hair, skin | Less change | Flag sign in hair, flaky-paint skin |
| Liver | Normal | Fatty, enlarged |
| Appetite | Good | Poor |

**Anthropometric terms (children)**

- **Stunting** — low height for age (long-term undernutrition).
- **Wasting** — low weight for height (recent, acute undernutrition).
- **Underweight** — low weight for age (both).
- **Severe acute malnutrition (SAM)** (WHO criteria): weight-for-height below −3 SD, or mid-upper arm circumference below 115 mm, or bilateral pitting oedema (age 6–59 months).

**Causes:** poverty, poor feeding practices, early stopping of breastfeeding, repeated infections (diarrhoea, measles, worms), large families, ignorance, food taboos, poor sanitation.

**Prevention**

1. Exclusive breastfeeding to six months; timely, adequate complementary feeding.
2. Growth monitoring; nutrition education of mothers.
3. Supplementary nutrition through Anganwadis (ICDS) and school meals.
4. Food fortification (iodised salt, fortified rice, oil and milk).
5. Vitamin A supplementation, iron–folic acid, deworming.
6. Immunisation, safe water, sanitation and hand washing to cut infections.
7. Family planning and women's education.
8. Kitchen gardens and income support for poor families.

## 1.10 Sociology and health

**Sociology** studies human society and behaviour in groups. Medical sociology looks at how social factors affect health and illness.

**Socio-cultural factors related to health and disease**

- **Culture and beliefs** — traditional healers, belief in evil spirits, use of home remedies, delay in seeking care.
- **Customs** — early marriage, early pregnancy, dietary taboos, open defecation habits.
- **Family** — joint or nuclear family, family support for sick and elderly, family size.
- **Religion** — fasting, diet rules, attitude to contraception and blood transfusion.
- **Social class and caste** — access to schools, safe water and health care.
- **Gender roles** — women's control over money and decisions on care.
- **Education** — mother's education is linked strongly with child survival.

**Impact of urbanisation on health**

Urbanisation is the movement of people from villages to cities.

| Positive effects | Negative effects |
| --- | --- |
| Better access to hospitals, specialists and pharmacies | Slums, overcrowding, poor drainage and water |
| More education and jobs | Air, noise and water pollution |
| Better transport and communication | Road accidents, injuries |
| | Sedentary life, fast food → obesity, diabetes, hypertension |
| | Stress, mental illness, drug and alcohol misuse, crime |
| | Spread of TB, dengue, HIV; breakdown of family support |

**Poverty and health — the vicious cycle**

```text
Poverty → poor food, housing, water, education
   ↑                         ↓
Loss of earnings  ←  Ill health and disability
```

Poverty causes disease, and disease (cost of treatment, loss of work) pushes families deeper into poverty. Breaking the cycle needs free primary care, insurance cover against hospital costs, nutrition support and safe water and sanitation.

## 1.11 Hygiene and health

**Hygiene** is the practice of keeping oneself and one's surroundings clean to prevent disease.

**Personal hygiene**

| Area | Good practice |
| --- | --- |
| Skin and bathing | Daily bath, clean clothes; prevents scabies and fungal infections |
| Hands | Wash with soap and water before eating, after toilet, after handling waste — the single most useful habit against diarrhoea and respiratory infections |
| Hair and nails | Clean hair, short nails; prevents lice and worm eggs under nails |
| Teeth and mouth | Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste; avoid tobacco and too much sugar |
| Eyes, ears, nose | Do not share towels or kajal; no sharp objects in ears |
| Feet | Wear footwear outdoors (hookworm); keep feet dry |
| Clothing | Clean, seasonal, loose clothes |
| Sleep, rest, exercise | Adequate sleep, daily physical activity |
| Menstrual hygiene | Clean pads or cups, change regularly, safe disposal |
| Food hygiene | Wash raw foods, cook well, cover food, safe water |
| Respiratory etiquette | Cover coughs and sneezes, no spitting in public |

**Health care at home:** first-aid box, safe storage of medicines away from children, checking expiry dates, proper disposal of unused medicines.

**Avoidable habits** (harmful habits that people can choose to stop)

| Habit | Health effect |
| --- | --- |
| Smoking and chewing tobacco (gutka, khaini) | Oral, lung and throat cancer, heart disease, COPD, poor pregnancy outcomes |
| Alcohol misuse | Liver cirrhosis, accidents, violence, family breakdown |
| Drug misuse | Dependence, overdose deaths, HIV and hepatitis through shared needles |
| Junk food, overeating | Obesity, diabetes, heart disease |
| Sedentary life | Obesity, hypertension, diabetes |
| Self-medication, especially antibiotics | Drug resistance, adverse reactions |
| Open defecation, spitting | Spread of worms, diarrhoea, TB |
| Unsafe sex | HIV and other sexually transmitted infections |
| Excess screen time, poor sleep | Eye strain, obesity, poor mental health |

**Role of the pharmacist in this unit:** health education on diet, hygiene and habits; screening for anaemia signs, obesity, high BP; supplying and explaining iron, folic acid, ORS and supplements; tobacco cessation advice; referring malnourished children to health services.

## Remember

- WHO (1948): complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease.
- Triad = agent, host, environment; NCDs are multifactorial.
- Levels of prevention: primordial → primary → secondary → tertiary (+ quaternary).
- Leavell and Clark: promotion, specific protection, early diagnosis, disability limitation, rehabilitation.
- Elimination ≠ eradication; smallpox is the eradicated example.
- Kwashiorkor has oedema; marasmus does not. SAM: WHZ < −3 SD, MUAC < 115 mm, or bilateral oedema.
- Vitamin A → night blindness, Bitot's spots; niacin → pellagra (3 Ds); C → scurvy; folate → neural tube defects.
- Poverty and disease form a vicious cycle; urbanisation brings both benefits and NCD/slum problems.
- Hand washing with soap is the most valuable personal-hygiene habit.
